design_critique: 1) The revision is close to the raced iteration-0 design (score 39.85, all 60 trials off track). Geometry is identical to iteration 0, and kp 5.0, ki 0 and last_direction are unchanged. The only changes are kd 0.02 to 0.05 and base_speed 1.7 to 1.5. Across iterations 0, 1 and 2, the outcome barely moved (every run had about 1 to 2 line-loss events, max_error about 0.06, progress 0.04 to 0.17), so this revision is expected to score about 39.85 or lower, not higher. The rationale does not predict a different result or explain why these two changes should break the failure pattern. 2) Lowering base_speed to 1.5 addresses the wrong failure. Progress is 0.04 to 0.17 on courses of about 4 to 5 m, so the robot leaves the line within roughly the first metre. Slower driving does not stop an early drift. It also cuts the progress rate, which makes the 3 s finish harder: at base_speed 1.5 the speed-to-time mapping is still unmeasured, and a 1.5 m/s average is required with no evidence that this demand produces that speed. 3) The most informative fact is ignored: the failure occurs early and is insensitive to kp (2.5 to 5), kd (0.02 to 0.1), sensor span, sensor size and speed (1.6 to 1.7). Fixed-cause candidates are the start transient (the robot begins on the line but at rest or with an initial heading error), the 2 percent left/right motor mismatch (offset about mismatch/kp, which is small at kp 5 but still uncorrected with ki 0), and a sensor or geometry error. None of these is tested by this design. 4) kd 0.05 is 2.5 times the raced value of 0.02, yet the rationale calls it staying near the raced value. The turn contribution is 100*kd*d, so 0.05 gives 5 turn units per unit signal change per second, about 0.1 turn units for a 0.02 step. That is probably harmless, but it is an unmeasured change that cannot be separated from the speed change in the same race. 5) Saturation check: base_pwm is 4095*1.5/2 = 3071, so the outer wheel has 1024 PWM of headroom and saturates near |signal| 0.59 at kp 5. That is adequate for the weights used, so the change does not cause a steering-loss problem. 6) The falsifiable target steering_oscillation below 0.16 is essentially the raced mean (0.161 to 0.177), so it does not discriminate between outcomes. The max_error target below 0.06 is the off-track boundary itself, so a pass means only not failing.
rationale_critique: 1) The claim that 1.5 is the nearest value to the finish requirement is not supported. The requirement (1.5 m/s average) is stated in ground-speed terms, but base_speed is a dimensionless drive demand (base_pwm = 4095*base_speed/2). The rationale mixes the two units, so the choice of 1.5 has no derived link to the finish requirement. 2) 'Keeps kd near the raced value' is inaccurate: kd moves by a factor of 2.5. The rationale should state this as a change, not as a near-unchanged value. 3) The rationale says the change set keeps the race attributable, but it changes two controller values at once (kd and base_speed), and the expected effects are not stated separately. It also does not say which to revert first if the race fails. 4) The rationale gives no prediction of the score or of completion. It only lists thresholds that the raced baseline already roughly meets or misses, so the race cannot tell the team whether the revision improved anything. 5) The rationale still cites geometry as the best lever (iteration 0 being the best raced geometry), but iterations 0 and 1 scored the same (39.8523 vs 39.8521) with different geometry and gains. The evidence supports the view that neither geometry nor gain tuning moved the score, and the rationale does not address that tension. 6) No fallback is given if the race fails to complete or stays off track at about 0.06 m. A better next step would be to log per-step telemetry for the first 100 steps (about 1 s) to locate the start transient, and to test the motor-mismatch offset directly with a small ki, since both are cheap to check and neither is tested here.
